newsitem.title: HUNGARY: HUNGARY SAYS RUSSIA STILL OPPOSED TO NATO ENLARGEMENT.
newsitem.headline: HUNGARY SAYS RUSSIA STILL OPPOSED TO NATO ENLARGEMENT.

text.p: Hungary on Wednesday welcomed Russia's decision to open talks with NATO on a special relationship but said this did not mean Moscow's opposition to enlargement of the alliance was any weaker.

"Russia still opposes the enlargement of NATO," defence ministry state secretary Istvan Gyarmati told Hungaiam television. "But it will have to accept it and to negotiate on this basis its future relations with an enlarged NATO."

The NATO allies, saying all of Europe stood to gain, hailed Russia's decision on Wednesday to open talks with NATO on a special relationship despite its deep hostility to alliance plans to expand eastwards.

In a major change of policy, Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov told his 16 NATO counterparts in Brussels that Moscow was ready to enter into dialogue on a new security partnership between the former Cold War foes.
Hungarian foreign minister Laszlo Kovacs told Hungarian television developments in Brussels led him to believe Hungary would be invited to join NATO early in 1999.
"Hungary's accession can be relatively clearly calculated for spring 1999," he said. "That is when the first group of new members will be officially accepted."
Hungary, Poland and the Czech Republic are the favourites to be invited to join out of a total of 11 countries now clamouring at NATO's door.
Kovacs added that he was not surprised by NATO's Tuesday statement declaring it would not station nuclear weapons on new members' territory.
"The alliance has previously indicated this position," he said. "The fact that NATO has so emphasised the point should be interpreted rather as a gesture towards Russia."

Earlier, Hungarian Prime Minister Gyula Horn said after meeting Italian President Oscar Luigi Scalfaro, who is on a state visit to Hungary, that it was Hungary's sovereign right to decide whether or not to join NATO.

He said the present form of cooperation between Hungary, Italy, and Slovenia was especially important and expressed the hope that Austria, which has repeatedly declared its neutrality, would also join.
Scalfaro pledged Italy's full support for Hungary's admission to both NATO and the European Union.
"Russia's worries about NATO enlargement should disperse soon as it is also Russia's interest to be in a politically secure region," he said.
